observer.description: nginx on the production host, as recorded by opsledger on the same host. These numbers are reported by the system they describe.

origin.method: Every request nginx handles is written as a JSON access-log record to a Unix datagram socket (nginx's syslog transport). opsledger parses each record, classifies it and aggregates it per minute (counts by outcome and status class, an exact latency-threshold count, and a base-2 exponential histogram of $request_time). Once a minute, opsledger also reads nginx's own request counter (stub_status) so that records lost in transit can be counted.
limitations: Requests answered by the CDN edge (cached static assets) never reach the origin and are not counted.
Outages that stop requests before nginx (DNS, CDN, network, host down) are invisible here; the external probe covers them partially.
$request_time has millisecond resolution and includes sending the response to the CDN, not the visitor's full page load.
The data is reported by the production host itself. A signed report proves which workflow published it and that it has not changed since, not that the host measured truthfully.

observer.description: A scheduled GitHub Actions workflow on GitHub-hosted runners, outside the production host and its network, requests public pages and the API over HTTPS through the CDN, like a visitor.

probe.method: Each scheduled run performs a fixed list of HTTPS checks (status, expected content, snapshot consistency between pages and the API, certificate validity) and records the result, timings and the probe's own source revision. A run succeeds only if every check succeeds. Results are uploaded as workflow artifacts and collected once a day.

limitations: The probe samples the site once per scheduled run; an outage that starts and ends between runs is not observed.
GitHub may delay or skip scheduled runs under load; missing slots are listed and are neither successes nor failures.
Runs come from GitHub's network only: one vantage point, not a representative sample of visitors' networks.
A success ratio of probe runs is not an uptime percentage; see the interval bounds and the zero-failure bound.
Recomputing this report proves that its statistics follow from its observations; it cannot prove the observations are true.
Small samples produce wide intervals; read every ratio together with its n and its interval.
